cim: Build an AI Agent From Scratch in Python: The Agentic Loop
cim_eredeti: Build an AI Agent From Scratch in Python: The Agentic Loop
szoveg_eredeti:
You know how LLMs work, and you may already use AI agents to help you write code. However, an LLM isn’t an agent. What sits between them is the agentic loop. In this tutorial, you’ll build an AI agent from scratch in Python by writing the harness that turns a language model into an agent. You’ll do this in about ninety lines of code, with no frameworks.

By the end of this tutorial, you’ll understand that:

You’ll start with a single call to an LLM, which fails at the very first task you give it. Each step that follows moves you closer to fixing that failure, until the model can explore a folder it has never seen and summarize what’s inside. Here’s a glimpse of the agent you’ll build, as it asks the harness to run two tools, one after the other, before it answers:

Agentic Loops Live Course: If you’d rather build an agent with an instructor, join Stephen in Real Python’s agentic loops live course. Over two live sessions, you’ll write the loop by hand and learn to predict what agents like Claude Code will do next.

Test your understanding of how an AI agent works in Python, from the harness and conversation context to tool calls and the agentic loop.

You should be comfortable with the following topics to get the most out of this tutorial:

You don’t need any experience with AI agents or agent frameworks. If you don’t have all of the prerequisite knowledge before you start, that’s okay. You can always stop and review the resources linked here if you get stuck.

You’ll talk to a model through the OpenAI Python library, so you’ll need an OpenAI API key. This tutorial uses Python 3.15 and uv to manage the project, so you’ll need to install uv if you don’t have it. You can create a project and add the library to it:

If you have Git installed, the uv init command also creates a Git repository with a .gitignore file. Before you save your API key anywhere, add .env to the end of .gitignore so that you don’t commit your key by accident:

Next, create a file named .env in the ai-agent/ folder and place your API key in it:

The OpenAI library reads your API key from the OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable. You can ask uv to load the .env file into the environment every time you use uv run in that terminal session by setting the UV_ENV_FILE variable. Select your operating system below:

Every API call in this tutorial costs a small amount of money, so you’ll need to set up billing for your OpenAI account. Throughout this tutorial, you’ll use gpt-6-luna, a capable, inexpensive model.

The downloadable materials include a folder called habits. Place it inside your ai-agent/ project folder, next to the script you’ll write. Your project should look like this:

The uv init command also creates a few other files, such as main.py and README.md. You won’t need them in this tutorial, so you can leave them alone or delete them.

You won’t look inside habits in this tutorial, and that’s on purpose. First, its contents don’t matter. Second, finding out what’s in it is the job you’ll give your agent.

Before you build anything around a model, you can see what it does on its own. In this step, you’ll send a single question to an LLM and print its answer.

The finished code for this step is in source_code_step_1/ in the materials you downloaded earlier.

Create a file named ai_agent.py and add the following code:

The OpenAI object is the client you use to talk to the models hosted by OpenAI. You’ll call client.chat.completions.create() every time you want to send something to the model. This method uses OpenAI’s Chat Completions API. You pass the name of the model and a list of messages.

Each message is a dictionary with a role and some content. The role tells the model who sent the message. In this case, you’re the user. Later in this tutorial, you’ll also see messages that come from the model itself and from tools. The messages argument is a list because a conversation usually has more than one message, even though you have only one so far.

The object returned by .create() has a .choices attribute. The name is plural because the API can return more than one response. However, you’ll ask for only one, so you can take the first item and fetch the text from its .message.content attribute.

You can run the script from your terminal:

You’ve sent a message to a language model and received a reply. However, the reply is a polite refusal. The model can’t read what’s in habits. In this request, all it can do is receive text and return text.

Your output will differ from the example shown here and from the output of any other run of the same script. LLMs rarely give the same reply twice. However, the overall message will be the same, and that’s what matters in this tutorial.

In the previous step, the model told you it couldn’t access your files. That’s true, and it’ll stay true. The model will never read a file directly. Instead, you’ll build infrastructure around the model to access files on its behalf. This infrastructure is the harness, and it starts as a plain while loop.

The finished code for this step is in source_code_step_2/ in the materials you downloaded earlier.

Instead of hard-coding a single question, you can let the user type messages in a loop. You’ll also move the model’s name into a constant so that you only need to change it in one place:

The while True loop is the harness. Notice the prompt in input(). You’re no longer sending your question directly to the model. You’re sending it to the harness, which builds the list of messages and passes it on to the model. When the reply comes back, it goes to the harness first, and the harness passes it on to you.

You’ll also notice that the reply is now the .message object itself, rather than its .content. You’ll need the whole object later in this tutorial.

The loop keeps running. You can stop it at any time by pressing Ctrl+C.

Before you run the script, you’ll add a helper function called trace() that prints a line every time information moves from one part of the system to another. You can call it just before the harness sends a message to the model and just after the reply comes back:

Each line that trace() prints shows who’s sending, who’s receiving, and a short description of what’s being sent. When the model replies, the trace shows the length of the reply rather than the reply itself, which keeps the output short.

You’ll build an agent with several moving parts, and most of what happens is invisible unless you print it. The trace lines make the flow visible, and you’ll read them after every run to follow what’s happening behind the scenes.

You can run the script and ask the same question as before:

You can follow the trace line by line. You send your question to the harness. The harness sends a message to the model. The model sends a text reply of 129 characters back to the harness, and the harness passes the reply on to you.

The model still can’t see the folder, which is no surprise since nothing has changed from the model’s point of view. However, the harness keeps running and waits for your next message. That’s where the next problem shows up.

The harness from the previous step lets you keep chatting since it has a while True loop. In the same session, you can ask a follow-up question that refers back to the folder. Here’s the whole session so far, with the new lines highlighted:
